..
As of 223 AM EST Friday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: An active weather pattern will be present through the 
next several days as shortwave troughs move through our region. The 
first of these is a slow mover; an upper level low will 
cross New York and Vermont from Saturday afternoon through 
Sunday morning, when highest chances of rain generally are on 
the table.

To start with for today, we are within a dry slot ahead of the first 
upper level low and a plume of deeper moisture along a developing 
coastal front. It appears on the northwestern fringe of this 
plume showers tracking over southeastern New York will likely 
slide through southern and eastern Vermont, with a batch of 
showers arriving by noon and exiting soon after. As a wave of
low pressure develops over southern New England, somewhat
heavier showers will develop; there remains quite a bit of
spread with how far west the rain will get. As such, have
maintained roughly 40-60% PoPs over eastern Vermont with a more
uncertain 0.1 - 0.3" of rain than typical in this time range.

Meanwhile, shower chances will increase Friday afternoon over 
western portions of northern New York as strong upper level 
divergence and some near surface convergent flow develops ahead 
of the aforementioned upper level low. Showers in this area 
will be light but persistent for much of the weekend, especially
towards southern St. Lawrence, Franklin, and Essex counties, 
and will gradually expand eastward into the south central 
Vermont. As the upper level low crosses to our south Saturday 
night, sufficient cooling for a changeover to snow in higher 
elevations is becoming a bit more likely. Probabilities of at 
least some snow mixing in with rain, even down to elevations as 
low as 1000 to 1500 feet if precipitation is heavy enough, are 
above 20%, especially over northeastern portions of Vermont and 
the northwestern Adirondacks. In a reasonable high end scenario 
given a timeframe falling during the nighttime hours, up to a 
couple inches of wet snow could accumulate in some towns above 
1500 feet.

The northward extent of rain showers, and potential for 
steadier rain particularly in the Saturday afternoon through 
Sunday morning timeframe, remains uncertain. The latest guidance
has trended wetter in northern areas including north central 
and northwestern Vermont. The potential for a good soaking rain,
with rainfall amounts in the range of 0.5"-1", would be tied to
a more rapidly deepening surface low pressure area in the Gulf 
of Maine and an associated deformation zone across western 
Vermont/northeastern New York that is favored due to terrain 
enhanced convergence. Precipitation chances generally look at 
their minimum for the weekend later Sunday as brief ridging 
builds in before another shortwave trough quickly approaches for
Sunday night. 

On Monday, the most noteworthy part of the forecast may be
related to seasonably gusty northwest winds as another trough 
swings through with typical cold season advection. Given the 
recent warm weather, this air mass will be notably chilly with 
apparent temperatures most likely in the 30s for most of the day
in many locations. Unlike over the weekend, guidance is in good
agreement on 850 millibar/mountain temperatures falling below
freezing (estimated snow levels around 2500-3000 feet), so if 
there is sufficient moisture for showers, there should be some 
light snow/flurries, as well.

KEY MESSAGE 2: A broad upper trough 
will remain fairly entrenched across eastern Canada for mid to 
late week. As a result, shortwaves will periodically pinwheel 
around the trough and move across our region, bringing rounds of
showers. There's some model consensus that by late week, one of
these will develop a closed low at mid/high levels while a 
surface low develops off the East Coast. This would point toward
cooler temperatures (the GFS has highs in the 30s and 40s by 
Thu/Fri), but there's still plenty of uncertainty given we're a 
week out. Have stayed with the WPC/NBM forecast for now, which 
while a bit on the warm side, does still indicate chances for 
nighttime snow showers over higher elevations, while 
precipitation should fall as rain during the daylight hours with
highs mainly in the 40s.
